question.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=1,$ we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{3x+2}-\sqrt{4x+1}} & =\frac{1-1}{\sqrt{3(1)+2}-\sqrt{4(1)+1}}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{3x+2}-\sqrt{4x+1}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(\sqrt{3x+2}+\sqrt{4x+1})}{(\sqrt{3x+2}-\sqrt{4x+1})(\sqrt{3x+2}+\sqrt{4x+1})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(\sqrt{3x+2}+\sqrt{4x+1})}{(\sqrt{3x+2})^{2}-(\sqrt{4x+1})^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(\sqrt{3x+2}+\sqrt{4x+1})}{(3x+2)-(4x+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{-(1-x)(\sqrt{3x+2}+\sqrt{4x+1})}{1-x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}[-(\sqrt{3x+2}+\sqrt{4x+1})] \\  & =-(\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{5}) \\  & =-2\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
